opus-5.5.text:
I think the influence is real, even though I never worked at Facebook myself. A number of the people who joined us early came out of Meta, especially from the research side, and they brought habits with them that shaped how we work from day one.

The biggest one is the bias toward shipping and iterating. "Move fast" gets mocked sometimes, but the core idea is right for a company like ours: you don't learn much from a beautiful plan. You learn from running the experiment, seeing it fail, and running the next one the same afternoon. In AI for math that matters a lot, because the space of ideas is enormous, and the only way through it is high-velocity experimentation with good infrastructure underneath.

The second is the open research culture that FAIR had. People published, shared code, argued in the open, and assumed that ideas get better when more smart people look at them. We've tried to keep that internally. Anyone can challenge anyone's approach, and a junior researcher with a good counterexample wins the argument against a senior person with a vague intuition. Math is very unforgiving that way, which I like. A proof either checks or it doesn't.

The third is small teams with a lot of ownership. One person or a pair can own a whole piece of the system end to end, and nobody waits for permission.

That said, we've consciously not copied everything. A big company can afford many parallel bets and a lot of reorganization. A startup can't. So we take the speed and the openness, but we're much more focused. We pick a few things we believe are true about where mathematical reasoning is going, and we go very deep on them. The way I'd put it: Facebook taught a lot of our people how to move fast, and our job is to make sure we're moving fast in one direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes Meta-influenced habits but does not compare Facebook’s bottom-up culture with Google’s top-down culture.

r002.rationale: It says a number of early joiners came from Meta and shaped the company’s work, but does not say most early founding employees transferred its culture.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say the influence is real but it's more indirect than people assume. I never worked at Facebook myself, so what I absorbed came secondhand, mostly through people who did, and through the broader culture it seeded across the Valley.

The piece that stuck with me is the obsession with speed as a value in itself. "Move fast and break things" became a cliché, but the deeper idea underneath it is that most of what you believe about your product is wrong, and the only way to find out which parts are wrong is to ship, measure, and iterate. When you're building a company around AI for mathematics, that turns out to be surprisingly relevant. You have a very strong temptation to sit in a room and reason about what mathematicians need, because the founders are mathematicians and we think we know. Facebook's culture is a useful corrective to that. Put it in front of users, watch what actually happens, be willing to be embarrassed.

The second thing is how they thought about talent density. Facebook in its early years was ruthless about hiring extremely strong engineers and then giving them a lot of autonomy. Small teams, owned end to end. I think that model fits us well, because the kind of people who can work at the intersection of frontier models and serious mathematics are rare, and if you find one, you don't want to put three layers of process between them and the problem.

But I'd also say we've consciously diverged in places. Facebook optimized relentlessly for engagement, and in hindsight a lot of people, including people who were there, feel that metric ate the mission. For us, the thing we care about is whether we actually produce correct mathematics and whether people trust it. Those are slow metrics. They don't move daily. So we borrowed the speed in how we build, but we're trying to be much more deliberate about what we measure, because the metric you choose ends up choosing your culture for you.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Facebook’s speed and talent practices but does not compare its organizational culture with Google’s.

r002.rationale: It says the influence came secondhand through people who worked at Facebook and the broader Valley, but does not say the company inherited its culture from most early founding employees.

astra-6.text: I think culture shows up most clearly in what a company rewards. Facebook is often associated with moving fast, and the part of that I find useful is giving people ownership and encouraging them to test ideas rather than wait for permission. But speed alone isn’t enough. You also need people to question assumptions and take responsibility for the consequences of what they build. So I’d think about that influence selectively: what helps our team learn faster, and what fits the company we want to become?

r001.rationale: The response discusses Facebook’s emphasis on moving fast, ownership, and testing ideas, but does not contrast its culture with Google’s.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that Carina Hong’s company inherited its culture from most of its early founding employees.

sol-6.1.text: I’d separate the parts of Facebook’s culture that are useful from the parts that depend on its scale. Moving quickly, giving people ownership, and testing ideas against real feedback can be valuable. But you also need room to question what you’re building and why. For our company, I’d want speed to come from clarity and trust, with people feeling comfortable raising concerns early. The point is to learn from Facebook without assuming its culture will fit us wholesale.
